 Regional perspectives on air quality and health: WHO Region of the Americas: technical brief
 Science and policy snapshots on air quality, energy and health
 18 November 2026 
  |  Technical document 
 Download (2.7 MB) 
 Overview 
 This technical brief examines air pollution and its health impacts in the WHO Region of the Americas, highlighting regional evidence, policy responses and priorities for action. Air pollution was responsible for approximately 411 000 deaths in 2021, while nearly 74 million people rely on polluting fuels for cooking and heating. Despite progress in air quality regulation, substantial gaps remain in monitoring coverage, health surveillance and access to clean household energy, with disproportionate impacts on vulnerable populations. 
 The brief presents national and local initiatives integrating air quality, climate action and public health, including urban interventions in Colombia, health impact assessments in Trinidad and Tobago, and clean household energy policies in El Salvador. Priority actions include strengthening monitoring systems, updating air quality standards, expanding clean energy access and building health sector capacity for intersectoral policy-making. Regional efforts emphasize integrated health impact assessments, evidence-based decision-making and coordinated action to improve air quality and protect public health.
 This document is part of the WHO Air Quality, Energy, and Health Science and Policy Summaries (SPS). These summaries provide concise overviews of current knowledge and evidence on air quality, energy access, climate change, and health. They aim to support decision-makers by presenting key insights from scientific research. 
 The SPS are developed through a multistakeholder consultation process that includes experts from WHO Advisory Groups – i.e., the  Scientific Advisory Group on Air Pollution and Health (SAG) , and the  Global Air Pollution and Health – Technical Advisory Group (GAPH-TAG)  – as well as specialists from  WHO Collaborating Centres , UN agencies as well as other experts from academia and civil society.
